target_customer: YouTube creators who want to sell branded merchandise, and their fans who buy it
problem: Creators wanted merchandise without managing production and fulfilment. FanHero applied a creator's image to posters, shirts and phone cases and handled sales.
business_model: Merchandise platform taking a commission on sales (creators kept all revenue in beta, share planned to fall to 75 percent after September 2013 per TechCrunch)

founders.name: Charlie Guo
education: Stanford University, computer science undergraduate (per TechCrunch 2013-07-18)
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as founder and says he is now a Developer Experience Engineer at OpenAI.

founders.name: Kevin Xu
education: Stanford University, computer science undergraduate (per TechCrunch 2013-07-18)
founders.background_notes: Named as founder by YC page and TechCrunch.

technical_complexity.rationale: Image to product mockup, storefront and print on demand fulfilment partners. Mostly integration work.

defensibility.rationale: Print on demand merchandise is easy to copy and the 2013 article names no proprietary asset beyond creator relationships.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Not documented for the original company.

market_need_then: TechCrunch (2013-07-18) described YouTube creators with large audiences but few easy ways to sell merchandise, and cited an example of a fan paying $50 for a $13 shirt. No spend data was found.

branding.domain_note: fanhero.com now serves a different company, a creator community and content platform with a CREATOR AI product, so domain history for the 2013 company is unknown.
branding.community_and_virality: TechCrunch coverage in July 2013 described a leaderboard of top buyers; no merch community or fan accounts found.

brand_strength.rationale: The name fits fan culture, but only launch coverage was found and the same name was later used by an unrelated creator platform.

outcome_analysis: FanHero joined YC in Summer 2013 and launched a merchandise tool for YouTubers in July 2013 with no disclosed traction. The YC directory lists it as inactive and Dealroom marks it closed, but no post-mortem, shutdown date or cause was found, so the cause of failure is not public and failure factors are left empty. Dealroom also reports about $125 thousand of seed funding from a single database entry.
notes: The funding round rests on a single database (Dealroom, via search snippet) with no date given. CB Insights lists $1.27M total including a PPP loan, which most likely belongs to a later unrelated Orlando company also named FanHero, so it is not recorded. The YC page lists team size 1 but two founders. A Dealroom page also describes a family messaging app, which conflicts with the TechCrunch description and was ignored. No competitors were named in the 2013 launch article and searches found no dated rivals, so the list is empty. fanhero.com currently belongs to a different product and does not represent the 2013 company.
